body:
# Independent audit: Grünbaum-level cap cover forces global BM rigidity


`candidate 92518b410f30446b`.
Result: **PASS**, with the intended meaning of a proper cut explicitly
being positive captured volume strictly less than the whole volume.
That wording clarification was sent to root. No mathematical gap was
identified in the proof.

## 1. Exact hypotheses and the initial circuit rank

The endpoint bodies and K are full-dimensional compact convex bodies,
y lies in int(K), and all cap boundaries pass through y. The source
cap fractions are exactly Gamma_d. The endpoint cuts are proper and
positive-volume, so every truncated endpoint body used in BM is
nonempty and full-dimensional. No empty-set BM convention is used.

A minimal positive circuit with m columns has rank m-1. For clarity,
if its kernel contained a vector beta independent of its strictly
positive dependence alpha, change the sign of beta so some beta_i>0
and take

    t=min_(beta_i>0) alpha_i/beta_i.

Then alpha-t beta is a nonzero nonnegative dependence with at least
one zero entry; its support is a proper subfamily with a strictly
positive dependence. This contradicts minimality. The nullity is
therefore one, and m<=d+1. This also rules out repeated positively
parallel directions: their coefficients could be merged while
removing one column. The proof in the source does not assume the
rank is d; it obtains that later from rigidity.

Positive dependence makes the closed caps cover the whole ambient
space. Their boundary mass for ordinary d-volume is zero throughout.

## 2. Captured equalities give the exact Minkowski midpoint

For each i the midpoint of the two compact full-dimensional endpoint
caps is contained in `((A+B)/2) intersect H_i`, which is contained in
`K intersect H_i`. The assumed equality and BM give equal positive
volumes at the two ends of this chain. Thus the inclusions are set
equalities, not merely almost-everywhere identities.

Indeed, a compact proper convex subset of a full-dimensional compact
convex body has smaller volume. A point outside the smaller closed
set can be strictly separated from it. Move that point a small
positive distance toward an interior point of the larger body; the
new point is interior and still strictly beyond the smaller support
plane. A small ball about it is disjoint from the smaller set and
lies in the larger one. This verifies the strict-volume fact used.

Taking the union of the cap equalities gives `K subset (A+B)/2`;
the given reverse containment proves equality. No whole-body volume
or equality assertion was assumed in this step.

## 3. The centroid and single-cap equality

Let g be the ordinary volume centroid of K. If one cap strictly
contains g, the parallel through-g cap removes positive volume:
a thin slab just below g lies inside an interior ball of K and
between the two distinct cut planes. Ordinary Grünbaum then makes
the original cap strictly larger than Gamma_d|K|, impossible.

Thus every `u_i.(g-y)<=0`. Their strictly positive weighted sum is
zero by the circuit, so every value is zero. All original caps are
centroid equality caps. This does not yet infer g=y from an
unproved full-rank hypothesis.

The only ordinary rigidity input is the classical single-cap
equality case of Grünbaum: K is a pyramid over a base parallel to
the cut, with its unique apex on the captured side. Its precise
orientation and height mean are recorded in
`candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c`, Section 1,
which was read for this audit. The argument does not invoke a
mixed-integer theorem or the desired global OC classification.

## 4. Distinct apex/base argument and the simplex conclusion

For a pyramid `K=conv(v,F)`, the apex v is extreme, the base F has
dimension d-1, and every other extreme point of K belongs to F.
Every extreme point of F is also extreme in K, because F is an
exposed face. These other extreme points therefore span the entire
base hyperplane. If the same apex were used in another pyramid
representation, its other extreme points would determine that same
hyperplane and the same oriented normal toward the apex. The two
directions would be positively parallel, which minimality excludes.
Thus distinct circuit caps have distinct apices.

With lambda_i the affine pyramid height, this proves
`lambda_i(v_j)=delta_ij`. Its gradient is a positive multiple of
u_i. Rescaling the circuit coefficients gives a strictly positive
weighted sum of the lambda_i with zero gradient, hence a constant.
Evaluation at every apex shows all weights equal that same positive
constant. Division proves `sum_i lambda_i=1` on the entire space.

Each lambda_i has volume mean 1/(d+1); this follows directly from
the pyramid section density proportional to `(1-t)^(d-1)`. Integrating
the preceding identity therefore gives m=d+1. Applying the lambda_i
to an affine dependence among the apices forces every coefficient
to vanish. The apices form a full-dimensional simplex, and the
lambda_i are its actual barycentric coordinates. Their nonnegativity
on K gives K inside that simplex, while all its vertices are already
in K. Equality follows.

The resulting simplex gradients span R^d, so the previously proved
orthogonality `u_i.(g-y)=0` now yields g=y. This supplies both full
normal rank and the asserted centroid identification without assuming
either at the outset.

## 5. The support-face proof of simplex indecomposability

Suppose `A+B=2K` for the obtained simplex K. Fix any decomposition
`2v_i=a_i+b_i`. For every normal uniquely exposing v_i, the support
identity forces a_i and b_i to attain the separate supports. Since
their exposed faces sum to a singleton, both faces are singletons.
The same fixed decomposition is therefore valid as the unique pair
throughout the whole open normal cone of v_i.

The union of the open vertex normal cones is dense: directions on
which two vertex scalar products tie lie in finitely many proper
hyperplanes. On that dense set `h_A=max_i w.a_i`, because the
appropriate a_i attains the support and every other a_j is in A.
Continuity of support functions gives this identity everywhere,
proving `A=conv{a_i}` by separation; likewise for B. Full dimension
makes each list of d+1 points affinely independent.

Each edge of a simplex is an exposed face in d>=2. For a vector w
exposing `[v_i,v_j]`, both a_i,a_j are in F_A(w) and both b_i,b_j
in F_B(w): their fixed decompositions attain the common support
identity. Since

    F_A(w)+F_B(w)=2[v_i,v_j],

differences of points in either face are parallel to the edge.
There is no need to assume the summand faces are edges beforehand.
The parallel scalar for `a_j-a_i` is nonzero by affine independence
and is positive by taking a direction uniquely exposing v_i; that
direction uniquely exposes a_i too. The identical argument applies
to B.

Write `a_i-a_0=t_i(v_i-v_0)`. Comparing the edge i,j relation in
the independent directions `v_i-v_0,v_j-v_0` makes all t_i equal
to one positive number lambda. The vertex equations then give

    A=v+lambda K,        B=-v+(2-lambda)K.

The positive edge orientation in B implies 2-lambda>0. Thus both
summands are positive homothetic simplices, and their exact volume
scaling proves whole-body BM equality. This part uses only compact
support functions, exposed faces, and simplex affine independence.

## 6. Scope

The source-cap value Gamma_d|K| is essential additional data. The
proper captured-side equality cover alone has the independently
verified quadrilateral counterexample. The theorem does not show
that a mixed-integer extremizer has these own-fiber fractions, nor
that globally critical mixed caps are ordinary equality caps. All
such global implications remain outside its conclusion.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
